title: The Bitter Lesson
author: Rich Sutton
blurb: General methods that ride on more compute keep beating clever, hand-built human knowledge, even when it hurts to admit it.

title: I'm so bad at billiards that I ended up in the hyperbolic plane
author: 2swap
blurb: Outer billiards: instead of bouncing a ball inside a table, you hop a point around the outside of a shape. Do it on a Penrose kite and the pattern of where it lands turns out to be a tiling of the hyperbolic plane.

title: Taste for Makers
author: Paul Graham
blurb: Good design is simple, timeless, suggestive and often slightly funny, and taste is something you can get better at.

title: London Digital Art Map
author: Peckham Digital
blurb: A map, a network diagram and a calendar of London's creative computing scene in one page: the venues and communities, what's on, and a form to add your own.

title: What Color Is Your Function?
author: Bob Nystrom
blurb: A parable about red and blue functions that explains how async splits a language in two, and why some languages avoid it.

title: The Law of Leaky Abstractions
author: Joel Spolsky
blurb: Every non-trivial abstraction leaks, so you still end up needing to understand whatever sits underneath it.

title: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names
author: Patrick McKenzie
blurb: A list of assumptions about people's names that break real systems. Each one sounds reasonable until you meet the exception.

title: Parse, Don't Validate
author: Alexis King
blurb: Push checks to the edges by turning loose input into types that can't be wrong. Once the data is parsed, the rest of the code gets to trust it.

title: Reflections on Trusting Trust
author: Ken Thompson
blurb: A compiler can hide a backdoor that survives even after it's removed from the source, so you can't fully trust code you didn't write.

title: A Plea for Lean Software
author: Niklaus Wirth
blurb: Software gets slower faster than hardware gets faster. An argument for smaller, simpler programs that do less but do it well.

title: The Grug Brained Developer
author: Grug
blurb: Complexity is the apex predator. A caveman voice makes old advice about saying no, small refactors and wariness of abstraction impossible to forget.

title: Out of the Tar Pit
author: Ben Moseley & Peter Marks
blurb: Most complexity comes from state and control flow. The paper proposes separating essential logic from everything accidental.

title: Semantic Compression
author: Casey Muratori
blurb: Write the concrete code first and only pull out reusable pieces once real patterns appear, rather than designing abstractions up front.

title: Magic Ink
author: Bret Victor
blurb: Most software is information software, and it should be designed like a great infographic rather than a control panel full of buttons.

title: The Cathedral and the Bazaar
author: Eric S. Raymond
blurb: Why the open, noisy way Linux was built worked better than careful central planning, and what that means for software projects.

title: An App Can Be a Home-Cooked Meal
author: Robin Sloan
blurb: A tiny messaging app built for one family. Software doesn't have to scale to be worth making, any more than dinner does.

title: Local-First Software
author: Ink & Switch
blurb: Seven ideals for apps where your data lives on your own device first, with CRDTs quietly handling sync and collaboration.

title: Choose Boring Technology
author: Dan McKinley
blurb: Every team gets a few innovation tokens. Spend them on what makes the product different, not on a shiny new database.

title: Up and Down the Ladder of Abstraction
author: Bret Victor
blurb: Understanding a system by stepping between concrete examples and abstract views, taught through interactive diagrams you can play with.

title: The Web's Grain
author: Frank Chimero
blurb: Stop fighting the edgeless, flexible nature of the screen and design with the material rather than against it.

title: Everything Easy Is Hard Again
author: Frank Chimero
blurb: Front-end tooling became so powerful that simple sites got complicated. A designer looks back at twenty years of building for the web.

title: Programming as Theory Building
author: Peter Naur
blurb: The real product of programming is the team's shared mental model, not the code itself, which is why handovers are so painful.

title: Learnable Programming
author: Bret Victor
blurb: A programming environment should let you see the state and follow the flow, instead of typing into the dark and hoping.

title: Things You Should Never Do, Part I
author: Joel Spolsky
blurb: Rewriting from scratch throws away years of hard-won bug fixes. Netscape is the cautionary tale.

title: The Rise of Worse Is Better
author: Richard P. Gabriel
blurb: Simple, slightly wrong designs spread faster than correct complex ones, and then get improved once everyone's using them.

title: Design as Participation
author: Kevin Slavin
blurb: Designers aren't standing outside the systems they make. They're participants inside them, alongside everyone else.

title: Write Code That Is Easy to Delete, Not Easy to Extend
author: tef
blurb: Good code is disposable code. Layer things so pieces can be thrown away without taking the rest down with them.

title: The Log
author: Jay Kreps
blurb: An append-only log turns out to be the quiet idea underneath databases, replication and stream processing.

title: Hints for Computer System Design
author: Butler Lampson
blurb: Rules of thumb for building systems, from keeping interfaces simple to caching answers and using hints to go fast.

title: Go To Statement Considered Harmful
author: Edsger W. Dijkstra
blurb: A short letter arguing that unrestricted jumps make programs hard to reason about. It started one of computing's longest arguments.

title: The Humble Programmer
author: Edsger W. Dijkstra
blurb: Programmers should respect the limits of their own minds and keep programs small enough to understand.

title: Big Ball of Mud
author: Brian Foote & Joseph Yoder
blurb: Why so much real software ends up as a haphazard tangle, and why that's often a rational outcome rather than a failure.

title: Growing a Language
author: Guy Steele
blurb: A talk that builds its own vocabulary as it goes, making the case that languages should be designed to grow with their users.

title: The Joel Test
author: Joel Spolsky
blurb: Twelve yes-or-no questions for judging a software team, from source control and daily builds to hallway usability tests.

title: Beating the Averages
author: Paul Graham
blurb: How Lisp gave Viaweb an edge, and the Blub paradox: you can't see what a more powerful language offers from inside a weaker one.

title: Teach Yourself Programming in Ten Years
author: Peter Norvig
blurb: Real expertise takes about a decade of deliberate practice, whatever the '21 days' book titles promise.
